fields.h1: Build an Interior Design Style Quiz That Saves Every Result
fields.hero_description: Take the eight-question interior design style quiz below, or build your own and keep each result in your own database.
fields.features_heading: What Makes an Interior Design Style Quiz Work
fields.features_subheading: Describe the quiz in one prompt. Emergent builds it, then changes whatever you describe next.
fields.feature_1:
Options mapped to styles, scored by count

Name the styles you want as results and Emergent drafts questions whose options each point to one style. The style picked most often wins, and you reword any question by prompt.
fields.feature_2:
A result screen that leads somewhere

Each style ends on its own screen: the name, a short read on the preference, and the next step you choose, such as a gallery, a booking link, or a product list from your catalog.
fields.feature_3:
Every finished quiz lands in your table

Answers, the result, and the finish time are saved as one row in a database you own. Filter rows by style before a season starts, or export the whole table whenever you need it.
fields.feature_4:
An email step you can turn off

Ask for an email before the result screen, or skip the gate entirely. When a finished quiz names a budget over a line you set, the app sends a Slack or email alert the same hour.
fields.feature_5:
Built for a phone, with no response caps

Visitors answer one screen at a time with a progress bar, and the quiz keeps accepting entries past any count, because Emergent puts no response caps on surveys or quizzes.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain now, your code later

Host the quiz on your own domain, included in Emergent and billed in credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and change anything in it directly.

fields.usecase_heading: What Four Teams Do With Quiz Results
fields.tab_content_1:
The first call opens on 3 Japandi boards

Berrow Interiors attaches the quiz to its consultation form. Camille Roy's request lands tagged Japandi, with a living room and a $14,000 budget, as one row on the project table. Designer Petra Lindqvist reads the row before the call and walks in carrying 3 Japandi boards instead of a blank questionnaire.
fields.tab_content_2:
The quiz sorts 90 buyers into 3 packages

Saddlewick Homes finishes every home in one of 3 packages. Each buyer takes the quiz before their design center appointment, and the result rides on the appointment card next to the lot number. This quarter, 64 of 90 buyers landed on Warm Modern, and the showroom now opens on that package.
fields.tab_content_3:
Boxes packed to match each style profile

Juniper Post packs a decor box for 1,100 subscribers, and the signup quiz gives each one a style profile. A Coastal profile gets the rattan tray; the brass candle set goes to Traditional boxes. Monthly returns dropped from 96 boxes to 41 after the switch, and each swap is logged on the subscriber's row.
fields.tab_content_4:
Every result picks its own gift guide

The Setwell List grew on one promise: take the quiz, get decor picks that match. The quiz tags each subscriber by result, 2,900 of 8,100 sit in Mid-Century, and the holiday gift guide goes out in 5 versions, one per style. The app reads the tag from the subscriber table and sends each person the right version.

fields.howto_title: How to Make an Interior Design Style Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to plan an interior design style quiz, map every answer to a style, and build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the styles your results will name
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Decide what happens after the result
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask about rooms people live in
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Keep every option concrete and even
fields.howto_step_1_des: Name the result styles first and keep to 4 to 6, because every question needs one option per style. Pick styles you can serve afterward: a gallery you can fill, products you can tag, or a finish package you sell.
fields.howto_step_2_des: A result screen that only names a style wastes the visit. Give each style a next step before you write questions: a consultation form, tagged products, or a guide signup. The destination decides which intake fields the quiz should collect.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask what someone keeps, not what they admire in photos. A question about the sofa they bought, the shelf they cleared, or the finish they chose reads taste better than one about dream homes, and it keeps every option concrete.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Tie each option to one style and word it as a real object, so a visitor picks between things instead of adjectives. If a test run never lands on one style, its options read as the safe middle choice; rewrite them.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Ask for room and budget last
fields.howto_step_5_des: Put one or two intake questions after the style questions, where finishing is close. A designer needs the room and a budget line; a store needs an email at most. Cut any field you will not read this month.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Test every path before you share it
fields.howto_step_6_des: Take the quiz once per style, answering for that style on purpose, and check each result screen, the saved row, and any alert you set up. Fix the wording wherever you hesitated: the place you paused is where a visitor quits.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Put the quiz where decisions start
fields.howto_step_7_des: Link it from the consultation page, the signup form, or the booking confirmation rather than a blog footer. Watch the results table for 2 weeks and compare styles: if one result never appears, revisit its options before you change the page.

plan.angle: The top 10 is consumer quizzes from designer blogs, a trade association, a TV network, and retail showrooms: every one ends at a style name and an email gate. None lets the visitor build the quiz itself. This page does both: a playable interior design style quiz on the page, then four businesses that put results to work in ways the top 10 never shows: a design studio that opens its first client call at the result instead of a blank questionnaire, a home builder that maps results to its finish packages, a decor subscription box that packs each box against the subscriber's style profile, and a decor newsletter that sends its gift guide in one version per style. Every result lands in a database the owner keeps, with no response cap.
